item.title: opencode isn't open enough; oh-my-pi is the right choice
item.description:
I’ve written a dozen posts recommending opencode. Today I’m retracting.

How I got here

Since January, opencode + Zhipu Coding Plan has been my daily driver. I wrote about how it saves money, how it dodges vendor lock-in, how to wire up MCP tools — you can dig a dozen such posts out of this repo:

  • High efficiency on a budget: my AI agent workflow — the opencode + Gemini money-saver combo
  • OpenCode config optimization notes — token and config tuning
  • MCP tools worth using — tooling recommendations
  • Automating GitHub PR code review with OpenCode + GLM-5 — CI automation
  • OpenCode plugin optimization — the plugin surface in depth
  • Three bugs in opencode’s LLM provider — early bug analysis

Three months ago, in From saving money to worry, I said “keep using it, but stay watchful.” Two months ago, in Switching from claude code to omp, I recommended opencode and omp side by side.

Four months in, I’ve fully changed my mind. Not because opencode got worse — because it showed me what the word “open” is actually worth.

Here’s the conclusion up front: opencode isn’t open enough; oh-my-pi (omp) is the right choice.

item.title: OpenCode's GitHub Actions Automation System: Engineering Practices Behind 27 Workflows
item.description:
opencode is a 160k-star AI coding tool with 27 workflow files in its .github/workflows/ directory. This number is not uncommon for open source projects, but what’s truly interesting is not the quantity, but the scope these workflows cover: from conventional CI/CD to AI-driven community governance, they’ve done almost everything GitHub Actions can do.

This article analyzes the design of these workflows by category, discusses the pros and cons of this level of automation, and shares insights for our own projects.

item.title: OpenCode Optimization Beyond Configuration — Plugin-Based Optimization
item.description: I previously wrote an article OpenCode Configuration Optimization Record, which addressed token consumption and context management issues. However, configuration optimization handles “how the model runs,” while “the quality of code when it’s half-written” is something configuration cannot manage. This article starts from my development process of the opencode-review plugin, discussing how opencode-review helps an agent review and improve its own code within a session, resulting in higher quality code entering the PR.

item.title: Does Self-Hosting an LLM Really Let You Use It Without Limits?
item.description:
Many people start thinking seriously about self-hosting an LLM not because of technical romance, but because API bills, rate limits, or compliance requirements have started to collide with real business constraints.

So a very natural question shows up: if the model runs on your own machine, does that mean you can finally use it without limits?

My answer is: no. Self-hosting a model does not mean unlimited freedom. It mostly means that many of the constraints and costs previously absorbed by the platform are now transferred to you.

But there is a more useful second question: once usage gets large enough, can self-hosting actually become cheaper?

The answer is: possibly, but under stricter conditions than many people expect.

item.title: Private Cloud for Small Companies
item.description:
Many friends want to know: What is the internal server situation and infrastructure of our small software development company?

Internal development clusters essentially solve the following issues:

  1. Git code management
  2. Data security and backup
  3. Multiple virtual machines providing development environments

To address the above problems, we adopt the following solution.

Hardware Configuration

We need to run approximately 10 virtual machine servers and 4 development machines simultaneously. If not counting electricity costs, I’ve kept the server hardware cost at around 5000 RMB, which has been running stably for 2 years.

item.title: Recently Discovered Useful MCP Tools
item.description:
Recently, I’ve been extensively using the opencode/claude code combination for development and have explored three particularly useful tools.

They address several issues:

  1. Parallel development on a single server; controlling tmux: tmux and tmux-mcp
  2. Preventing claude code from stopping at meaningless points: ralph-loop
  3. End-to-end automated testing: playwright mcp

Tool List

tmux mcp

First, configure tmux in the Linux environment with opencode, then have opencode install https://github.com/rinadelph/tmux-mcp.git. Once installed, you can use oc to control tmux content.
